title: Who gets the proceeds from the AI listing wave?
summary: A billion dollars of shares sold to the public can finance a company's next investment, pay an early shareholder for taking risk years ago, or do some of each. Only the first use puts new loss-absorbing capital on the company's balance sheet. Both can increase the number of shares available to index investors. That distinction runs through Daniel Dieckelmann, Lavinia Franco, Paraic O’Gorman and Chiara Scommegna's analysis of the US listing boom and its implications for euro area investors. Their concern is what happens to funding when buyers lose their appetite, especially if issuers have already accumulated debt.

How much equity has actually been issued? Chart C.1 compares completed offerings with prospective ones. SpaceX had listed by the authors' information cutoff of 10 November. Anthropic had filed an amended registration statement but its shares had yet to trade. OpenAI's listing was expected in 2027. A July market estimate put US initial public offering (IPO) proceeds in 2026 at $225 billion, versus about $44 billion in 2025. ECB staff's later estimate was $212 billion. It combines January–October proceeds with an allowance for ordinary November–December issuance based on historical seasonality and a separate estimate for Anthropic. The difference between the estimates matters less than their shared sensitivity to a handful of exceptionally large deals. Neither is a realised annual total. Chart C.1's separate series on net public issuance deducts repurchases and extends only through the second quarter. Gross IPO proceeds alone cannot establish that the US corporate sector has become a net issuer for the full year.

Private capital allows businesses to grow larger before listing. Chart C.2 contrasts venture financing and age at IPO with successive private valuations of three technology companies. Private funding rounds reprice companies intermittently. An IPO makes the price widely visible and transfers risk from venture investors to a broader set of holders. The authors report that primary offerings accounted for 76% of IPO offerings in 2023–26. In a primary tranche the firm receives cash and outstanding shares increase. In a secondary tranche the selling shareholder receives the proceeds. The distinction also applies to follow-on offerings by already listed companies. A sale can deepen the public market and facilitate venture exits without improving the issuer's ability to meet repayments. New equity that actually reaches the issuer has no maturity, so unlike a debt refinancing it creates no later rollover requirement.

Could issuance warn of a correction? The quarterly comparisons in Chart C.4 relate IPO volume relative to GDP to market returns over the following two years. The fitted relationship slopes down in both markets, but explains only 10.5% of variation in US forward returns and 5.3% in the euro area. At firm level, IPOs of at least €1 billion returned a median 5.0% against a 1.0% market return after one month, then 7.6% against 9.7% after one year. Smaller offerings roughly matched the market at one year, with 12.1% against 12.6%. The sample comes from past and present constituents of two indices and the comparison uses issuance-volume and market-capitalisation weights. It cannot date the next correction. Lower discount rates can rationally raise today's share prices, encourage companies to list and imply lower future returns. Better expected investment opportunities or concern that tomorrow's window may close can also bring issuance forward. The earnings yield plotted against credit yields in Chart C.3 uses observed earnings and prices. It does not measure investors' required return directly.

The most distinctive test concerns who will absorb the shares. A passive fund tracking a float-adjusted index may need to buy when a larger float raises a company's index weight. A primary sale and an insider sale can both generate that demand. Passive ownership is first observable after a firm lists, so the authors' own estimates in Chart C.5 concern follow-on offerings. They study 1,990 current or former US and euro area index constituents, with usable passive ownership from January 2014 to July 2026. Increases in passive ownership over twelve months are associated with a higher chance of an offering over the same span. Among offerings that actually occurred, one percentage point more passive ownership one month earlier is associated with an issue about 3% larger. Controls include size, liquidity, profitability, leverage, trailing share returns and time effects. The weaker relationship when passive ownership falls suggests that firms do not symmetrically withdraw shares. Such declines account for about a tenth of observations, so the two directions are supported by different amounts of evidence.

These results speak more directly to listed issuers than to the current pipeline of private firms. For the latter, the authors cite a separate study in which firms expecting accelerated index inclusion raised about 6% more capital than comparable listings. The relative price advantage disappeared within roughly three weeks of entry. Eligibility matters because Nasdaq and FTSE Russell can admit large IPOs rapidly, whereas the S&P 500 still requires at least a year of trading. A temporary listing premium, durable cheap capital and increased insider sale proceeds are three different outcomes. The study gives reasons to track all three rather than treating a first-day price as a verdict on the investment.

Europe has not experienced a comparable IPO boom, yet its investors own substantial US equity. A US correction can lower household wealth, although concentrated ownership among wealthier households limits the likely consumption response. A more serious financing channel opens if debt or contractual commitments continue to rise while the equity window closes. Capital spending would then depend on refinancing or internal cash flows at the very time lenders turn cautious. The authors judge direct stability risk from issuance limited. Their argument for Europe's savings and investments union rests partly on an opportunity to deepen equity markets that can finance losses and investment across the cycle. The more that demand depends on correlated index flows, the more important it becomes to test whether equity will still be available when valuations fall.

questions.question: How much cash from each large offering actually funds the company?
questions.detail: Separate primary and secondary tranches, trace primary proceeds to investment or debt repayment, and compare them with scheduled repayments and contracted spending. A large float increase accompanying little new issuer capital would matter for index demand and the distribution of losses, but say little about resilience to a funding squeeze.

questions.question: Does faster index entry change the quantity of capital raised or merely the price at entry?
questions.detail: Compare similarly sized issuers qualifying under different index rules and follow primary proceeds, insider sales and prices beyond the three-week reversal window cited in the article. Eligibility itself depends on size, liquidity and float. Accounting for those features is essential before attributing any remaining difference to passive demand.

questions.question: When does high issuance add information about subsequent returns?
questions.detail: Repeat the two-year comparison with the largest listings removed and with starting earnings yields, credit yields and funding conditions observed at the time. This would test whether the relationship survives the influence of a few mega-deals and whether a plausible change in discount rates can account for it without an exuberance explanation.

questions.question: Which European exposures would turn a US equity correction into a financing problem?
questions.detail: Distinguish mark-to-market losses for well-capitalised holders from debt or commitments payable before operating cash flows arrive. Pair that schedule with evidence on whether euro area issuers could still raise primary equity under weaker fund flows. Losses on existing shares and the disappearance of funding for new investment have different economic consequences.
